title: Anthropic becomes one of world's most valuable public companies in stock market debut
text:
Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after its shares began trading on the stock market, taking its valuation to roughly $1.76 trillion (£1.34 trillion).

The artificial intelligence (AI) company's Thursday debut on the Nasdaq stock exchange was a crucial test for the industry, given the huge amount of money being poured into advancing the technology.

Anthropic's shares flew past its allocation price of $83 each , showing there was plenty of excitement around AI.

Yet the company, which is behind AI chatbot Claude, will remain under intense scrutiny in the months ahead to answer the key question surrounding AI: is it all worth it?

In just a few hours of trading, Anthropic's stock seemed to show that investors remain uncertain of where exactly AI is heading. The share price rose immediately to $111.53, sending the company's market value to almost $2 trillion, before falling by the end of the day as the shares closed at $97.17.

Some investors said Anthropic's debut seemed to be a success, as shares rose roughly 17% during the day, but the broader tech market did not perform as well.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index closed down nearly 2.3%. Stocks fell in the largest tech firms, including Google's parent company Alphabet, which was down by 2.9%, while Amazon lost almost 3.9%.

The buildout happening around this era of AI is among the most expensive endeavours in the history of technology, with more than $1 trillion being spent in the last year alone by a handful of major tech companies.

The speed at which investment has grown has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble.

"Bubbles don't burst on the day of the largest deal," Richard Whittle, an economist with the University of Salford said. "They burst later, if the positive future becomes suspect."

While the basics of the technology have been around for decades, the more recent advent of more powerful computers and related components have allowed the processing of more data than ever.

The result has been AI chatbots that simulate human speech and operate more quickly tasks like software coding, digital image generation, and searching the internet.

It represents a new way of using computers that has led to the rapid rise of Anthropic, which started just five years ago and is best known as the maker of the popular AI chatbot Claude.

As the first purely AI company to go public, Anthropic will almost certainly see significant swings in price on the stock market going forward, according to Ben Barringer, who leads technology research at Quilter Cheviot.

The "initial exuberance" will wear off, Barringer said, pointing to what happened with SpaceX earlier this year.

That company, led by Elon Musk, saw shares jump by about 10% on the first day of trading, taking the company to a record-breaking valuation of $2.2 trillion.

Within a month shares had fallen below their debut price, and have mostly fallen further since.

Most tech companies see their shares fall after hitting the stock market, often after reporting quarterly results for the first time.

But many such companies, including Meta, Amazon and Google, have gone on to become the largest and most profitable corporations in the world.

With Anthropic, investors are not only looking at a notable tech company with a major valuation, and a potentially big future in business, but a company that is the first of its kind on the stock market.

"There's no obvious peer to compare it to," Neil Wilson, an investor strategist at Saxo UK, said.

Simon Jack: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?

So, as individual investors and even researchers and investors at large funds ask themselves if Anthropic is really worth more than $1.7 trillion, or even more, there will be few answers available.

"We'll have a stab at it," Wilson said. "I don't think anyone really knows."

A few things will likely impact the company's success on the stock market in the near-term.

One of those things is the prospect of new laws governing the use of AI tools. In the US, where Anthropic is based, Democrats will be in many more positions of power come 2027, and several politicians have already said they will be looking to ensure AI tools are safe and have some guardrails attached.

Such regulation is currently unlikely at the federal level. US President Donald Trump on Thursday spoke about AI during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China, alongside Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.

Trump reiterated his position against "any form of robust regulation" around the technology, adding, "we won't allow that to happen, frankly."

The same day, however, a bipartisan group of US lawmakers formed the House AI Safety and Innovation Caucus, which will work specifically on AI regulation and safety considerations.

A significant driver of this kind of scrutiny is Anthropic itself. Company executives, including co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei, have been outspoken in their purported fears that future AI tools will become so capable they will outsmart humans, to the point where extinction is possible.

Anthropic has always put itself forward in public as an AI company that takes the safety of its technology very seriously.

Daniela Amodei, Anthropic's president and sister of Dario Amodei, boasted on Thursday that the company "had an AI safety team before we launched our first product".

Despite the company's claims that the technology it is building at a rapid pace could be dangerous, Anthropic has made one of the quickest trips from start-up to IPO in history.

title: California targets Nvidia in China AI chip probe
text:
California has served an investigative subpoena on the AI chip designer Nvidia in the wake of a scandal that ended in the departure of longtime CEO Jensen Huang.

The state's top law enforcement officer, attorney general Rob Bonta, said he is probing whether Nvidia or Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information, adding that such actions could violate California law if the company is found to have mislead investors and the public.

The BBC has contacted Nvidia for comment.

"Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta said on Thursday.

Nvidia has its global headquarters in Santa Clara, California.

Earlier this month, it emerged that Huang had an extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang, who was an executive at the Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed.

Some members of the US Congress have urged the Department of Commerce to investigate whether Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer, diverted Nvidia chips to China.

Megaspeed has previously said it is aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".

Nvidia shares have plummeted 22% since the New York Times reported on the affair in early November.

Earlier this week, the company's board chair Harvey Jones said Nvidia had no intention of reinstating Jensen Huang after the longtime Nvidia boss and co-founder issued a statement saying he would be "honoured" to return, as some tech leaders including Elon Musk campaigned on his behalf.

Huang has acknowledged engaging in extramarital affairs – and left the company last week after reports that he had relationships with subordinates.

title: F1 to introduce full-time race stewards from 2027
text:
Formula 1's governing body the FIA is to introduce permanent race stewards from the 2027 season.

The move follows consistent calls from grand prix drivers for the change because of criticisms of inconsistency of decisions regarding penalties for on-track incidents.

The FIA said in a statement that it would begin recruiting permanent stewards, and was planning a "phased introduction" during the 2027 season.

The FIA statement added: "The introduction of dedicated full-time stewards to the FIA's flagship championship will provide continuity and expertise within the stewarding structure, further advancing the FIA's commitment to fairness through the ongoing review and continuous improvement of sporting regulations and stewarding guidelines.

"It will also allow for deeper implementation of best practice and greater consistency in decision-making."

It said that the use of driver stewards, usually an ex-F1 driver, would continue, "recognising the invaluable expertise they bring".

The plan is for "a small number" of full-time stewards to be recruited during 2027 and the group to be expanded from 2028.

"Existing FIA stewards will continue to play a vital role, contributing their experience within a mixed roster of full-time and part-time stewards for the foreseeable future," the statement said.

In reality, the move is not a major step on from the current situation, where a small number of stewards are rotated around races.

Each grand prix has a group of four stewards, one of which is an ex-driver.

Current drivers have often referenced the fact that they had repeatedly complained during briefings with FIA officials that rulings on driver standards and racing errors were not applied on a consistent basis.

Last year, Williams driver Carlos Sainz, a director of drivers' body the Grand Prix Drivers' Association, said: "F1 and the FIA all agree that [permanent stewards] should be the way forward, where at least two of the three stewards are permanent and we have one rotational for teaching purposes."

The decision follows the opening of an FIA race operations centre at F1's Biggin Hill headquarters in south London.

The FIA has in recent years received increased income from F1 - which provides the majority of its funding - on the basis that this would be applied to improving officialdom and rule-making.

FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem said: "This latest major investment in FIA officiating reflects our dedication to delivering the highest standards of decision-making, fairness and integrity in motorsport.

"The recruitment of full-time stewards is a significant step in our longstanding mission of building a dedicated officiating ecosystem in the FIA Formula 1 World Championship, it is also an investment in the future of our sport."

title: ‘It Would Be Great to Win All Three’: Chloé Dygert Dreams of Gold Medal Sweep at the LA 2028 Olympics
author: ahood
text:
Dygert, second from left, was part of the gold medal-winning team in Paris. (Photo: Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images)

Chloé Dygert may be leaving the WorldTour, but she’s keeping her foot on the accelerator with an ambitious target of three medals at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics .

Dygert told Velo she’s aiming to defend Team USA’s team pursuit title and chase the time trial and road race at LA 2028.

With the Games less than two years away, the 29-year-old is already building toward a possible gold medal trifecta that could make her one of the breakout stars in Los Angeles.

“Of course it would be great to win all three, the time trial for sure, and then the road race would be just a total bonus,” Dygert told Velo . “I gotta be realistic here, so winning the time trial and obviously coming back and winning the team pursuit would be huge.”

As one of America’s most successful Olympic cyclists , Dygert already owns four Olympic medals. She won team pursuit gold and time trial bronze at Paris 2024, adding to her team pursuit bronze from Tokyo 2020 and silver from Rio 2016.

Qualifying comes first. Then she has to hit her peak across two disciplines in the summer of 2028.

Speaking to Velo’s Hannah Knapp at El Tour de Tucson, Dygert was already putting down some training sessions on the outdoor track.

“So for how the Olympics works, it kind of goes by body count rather than like the event itself,” she said. “I’m for sure gonna do the track team pursuit as long as we qualify and then hopefully the time trial and then by doing the time trial, I have to do the road race, so I’ll be doing three events.”

Two medals in Paris, so why not three in Los Angeles?

Dygert’s road to Los Angeles will run through the United States.

This week she confirmed she’s returning to Virginia’s Blue Ridge TWENTY28 after six seasons with Canyon SRAM in the WorldTour.

Dygert has been through the wringer with injuries and health setbacks. Her time trial crash at the 2020 world championships in Imola, where she suffered a devastating injury to her left leg, still divides her career into before and after.

“I’ve spent my time in Europe and gave it the best shot that I could. Before my accident, that was the plan,” Dygert said. “I wanted to go to Europe and I wanted to win everything in Europe. I wanted to be the best in Europe.

“But because of the accident, unfortunately some of those goals got derailed. I think it was very obvious that I just was never going to be the athlete that I was before the accident.”

Dygert returns to Nicola Kramer’s Continental team where she raced as a junior a decade ago.

“So now it’s all about what do I do going forward, how do I make the best of who I can still be, and that is why I’ve decided to come back to America,” Dygert said.

“I’m coming back to something that I’m familiar with, coming back to a team that supports me and my goals,” she said. “I want to win the worlds. I want to win the Olympics, and I’ve done that before with her, and so what a better team to come back to.”

Dygert is one of USA Cycling’s best shots at gold on home roads in 2028.

The two-time world time trial champion took bronze against the clock in Paris, and she heads into the Los Angeles Olympics with a title to defend on the track and a third chance at a medal in the road race. Here’s how all three stack up.

1. Defend gold in the team pursuit Dygert has been at the heart of the U.S. team pursuit for three straight Olympics, with a medal each time and a breakthrough gold in Paris. She skipped the track worlds last month, but told Velo the pursuit is still front and center in her plans for LA28.

Team USA has work to do. The Americans finished ninth in qualifying at the Shanghai worlds, more than three seconds shy of advancing. Kristen Faulkner was the only rider from the Paris gold medal quartet on the start line in China.

Only eight teams will start in Los Angeles. Great Britain won gold in Shanghai ahead of Italy and Germany, a reminder of how deep the field is. The Americans will have to earn their place first.

If they can find their Paris speed again, they’ll be in the medal fight.

2. Win gold in the individual time trial This is her other big target.

Dygert has won two world time trial titles, and she was less than a second from Olympic silver on slick roads in Paris. Grace Brown was in a league of her own that day, beating Dygert by more than 90 seconds. Just 0.87 seconds separated Dygert from silver medalist Anna Henderson.

The course will matter. Organizers have confirmed a start at the LA Zoo and a finish at Griffith Observatory, with the full route still to come.

How much climbing comes before that finish could shape Dygert’s chances of turning bronze into gold.

3. Take a shot in the Olympic road race First, Dygert needs a spot on the road team.

The United States has two guaranteed road race places per gender as host and can earn up to four per gender through the UCI nations rankings.

The road race is the longest shot, but Dygert has the engine for a long, hard race in national colors.

She finished 31st in the Olympic road race in Tokyo and 15th in Paris. She was fourth in 2019 and second at the 2024 worlds in Zürich to show what she can do when she’s in the mix at the finish.

Man hired by Russia spied on Silicon Valley tech and defense company, feds say
author: Dan Goodin
text:
A Russian national has been indicted on suspicions he was a Russian spy who stalked and surveilled employees of a Silicon Valley company that was assisting Ukraine in its ongoing war with its eastern neighbor.

Igor D’iu, 25, allegedly photographed the employees and their computer screens as they worked at a coffee shop located near the company’s Palo Alto office, federal prosecutors said Wednesday . He also kept a list of home addresses of employees and a senior executive. At one point, prosecutors said, D’iu trailed an employee as she traveled home from Palo Alto to San Francisco. An affidavit filed in the case referred to the employee as FEMP1, short for female employee, and said the event left her “in a state of emotional distress.”

Evasive and irregular turns

“FEMP1 made evasive and irregular turns, took back roads, and turned into a grocery store parking lot where D’IU continued aggressively following her vehicle,” an FBI special agent wrote. “D’IU followed FEMP1 through U-turns, illegal left turns, and ran a red light to stay with FEMP1 for nearly thirty miles. FEMP1 called 911 while driving and was instructed to drive directly to San Francisco Police Department (“SFPD”) Mission Station. Near SFPD Mission Station, FEMP1 flagged an SFPD patrol vehicle and reported the incident. D’IU left once FEMP1 made contact with the patrol vehicle.”

title: Traumatized teens sue school, cops after Doritos bag triggers AI gun alert
author: Ashley Belanger
text:
In October 2025, four Black high school students were sharing Cool Ranch Doritos after football practice, winding down and waiting for their rides home. It was then, in the lull of a moment any teen with after-school activities knows well, that the school’s AI gun detection system suddenly flagged one teen holding a bag of chips as a potential gunman.

Within two minutes, Baltimore County Public Schools officials who reviewed security camera footage linked to the alert determined there was no actual threat. They recognized the Doritos bag and canceled the alert, which notified not only other school officials but also the Baltimore County Police Department that no response was needed.

The false alert could have ended there—before a traumatizing campus clash with police—but it didn’t.

title: Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn?
author: Dan Milmo and Aisha Down
text:
The company counts physicists, a former journalist and an associate of the pope among its guiding lights

The paper fortunes of Anthropic’s seven co-founders reached a total of more than $180bn on Thursday as shares in their company started trading at a price ahead of expectations.

The opening price of $111.50 (£85) per share valued the entrepreneurs’ stakes – including the chief executive, Dario Amodei, and his sister Daniela – at between $26.5bn and $27bn each. The founders have pledged to donate 80% of their shareholdings in Anthropic to philanthropic causes, which would equate to about $150bn at the current share price.

Other investors generating considerable wealth from the float and the late share price surge include Madonna’s manager, Guy Oseary, whose venture capital firm, Sound Ventures, which he co-founded with Hollywood actor Ashton Kutcher, reportedly owns 0.5% as an early investor. That stake would be worth $10bn at the opening price.

At the closing price of $97.17, the combined co-founders’ stakes had fallen in value to just over $160bn at around $23bn each. The Sound Ventures stake was worth about $8.75bn.

Anthropic has also committed 5% of its shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, which will “explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations”. The company has said some of the proceeds could be used to address AI’s impact on the job market , though fears the technology will lead to significant job losses have yet to be realised.

Anthropic’s IPO is widely expected to channel vast sums into the coffers of a powerful social movement called effective altruism, via the many millions of dollars that its 5,300 staff will have made from the flotation. EA, as it is known, crystallised on university campuses in the US and UK in the early 2010s. It encourages its members to donate a substantial portion of their income to a set of specific causes that it deems high-priority. These include things like pandemic prevention, biorisk, nuclear safety and – overwhelmingly – the risks posed by advanced AI.

Anthropic’s co-founders, including Dario Amodei, are associated with EA. Amodei took a pledge to donate his income through the organisation Giving What We Can, which is associated with the movement. However, he now disavows his association and has said he does not consider himself an effective altruist.

In 2023, he told The New York Times’ Hard Fork podcast he was “sympathetic to a number of the ideas” promoted by EA, but against “dividing people up into tribes”.

Anthropic’s San Francisco-born chief executive was educated at Stanford and Princeton universities. He worked at the Chinese tech firm Baidu and then at Google before joining OpenAI, the developer of ChatGPT and now Anthropic’s arch-rival, where he had a key position as vice-president of research.

In 2020, Amodei left OpenAI, and it has been widely reported that his departure was due to conflicting views over safety. “It is incredibly unproductive to try and argue with someone else’s vision,” he said years later.

AI safety remains a major concern for Amodei. He called for a slowdown in AI development in September after the resignation of an employee who cited concerns AI could wipe out humanity and triggered a wave of concern about the existential threat posed by the technology.

Amodei is also blunt about the potential impact of AI on jobs, claiming that AI could eliminate half of all white-collar jobs by the end of the decade.

Amodei, Dario’s sister, began her career in politics, working in Congress and on a congressional campaign, before switching to tech and taking a job at Stripe, the payment processor. She moved to OpenAI before co-founding Anthropic with her brother. She leads teams on AI model safety and alignment , making sure AI systems adhere to human aims and values.

Like other Anthropic employees and co-founders, Amodei is tied to the EA movement. She is married to one of its major donors, Holden Karnofsky, who co-founded GiveWell and the major grant-giving organisation Open Philanthropy.

This Brighton-born former journalist has been catapulted into the list of richest Britons with the Anthropic flotation. His paper wealth of approximately $26.6bn (£20.3bn) compares with £38bn for the London-based Hinduja brothers and puts him above the £18.2bn fortune of the Reform UK donor Christopher Harborne and Manchester United’s co-owner Jim Ratcliffe, who is worth £15.2bn. Clark leads the Anthropic Institute, a thinktank devoted to researching the social implications of advanced AI.

In a lecture at Oxford University this year, Clark predicted that an AI system will work with humans to make a Nobel prize-winning discovery within 12 months, and that tradespeople will be helped by bipedal robots within two years. He added that it would be better if humans could slow the development of the technology “to give ourselves more time as a species” to deal with the implications of its powers.

Anthropic’s chief science officer received a PhD in theoretical particle physics from Harvard before working as a researcher at OpenAI, then co-founding Anthropic. He is known for his work on scaling laws – the idea that AI models grow smarter and more powerful in proportion with the resources that are spent on training them.

In an interview with the Guardian last year, Kaplan focused on the major AI safety concern that animates much of Anthropic’s work – the power and potential risk of AI systems that can improve themselves. Creating such systems would be “the ultimate risk,” he said.

Anthropic’s chief compute officer, who is in charge of the company’s use and procurement of datacentres, was a senior engineer at OpenAI. Given his job title, he is unsurprisingly supportive of a divisive topic in US politics: whether to build more datacentres. Speaking in September, Brown praised Donald Trump’s social media post stating “let data reign”.…

title: Pochettino's first Man Utd training session filmed by drone operator
text:
Manchester United fans have been given a unique and unexpected insight into Mauricio Pochettino's first training session after footage was captured by a drone flown next to the club's Carrington training ground.

Twelve minutes of the session was filmed by a drone operator and uploaded onto YouTube.

Pochettino and his players, who were split into three groups, are clearly visible, with the session filmed from a variety of angles and distances.

"For the people asking about legality. It is unrestricted airspace, meaning anyone can fly over it," said the drone operator.

"The drone remained in line of sight at all times, it didn't fly over anyone or even near anyone so was a perfectly legal flight going by the CAA rules that regulates drone usage.

"The drone is correctly labelled, and I hold all the relevant licences, public liability and insurance required. As for leaking team news/tactics, it was half an hour into the managers first training session, there are many media there so certainly won't be the only footage of training released."

The session was also filmed by United's own media channel, who regularly film club training sessions.

Civil Aviation Authority guidelines include the following warning: "If you use these devices where people can expect privacy, such as inside their home or garden, you're likely to be breaking data protection laws."

Manchester United have declined to comment.

There were 10 outfield players working with Pochettino, although it seems unlikely it will be the starting line-up for Sunday's trip to Liverpool.

While Harry Maguire, Kobbie Mainoo, Amad Diallo, Matheus Cunha and Bryan Mbuemo are regular starters, Ayden Heaven and Andrey Santos have had less involvement, while neither Joshua Zirkzee nor Harry Amass have started a Premier League game this season.

On an adjoining pitch, skipper Bruno Fernandes is shown in one group playing the 'Rondos' game, where two players are in the middle trying to intercept the passes of the five players in a circle on the outside. Youngster Shea Lacey and last season's FA Youth Cup-winning skipper Dan Armer are also involved, along with England youth international Bendito Mantato.

Next to that is another group which includes more experienced players in Lisandro Martinez, Matthijs de Ligt, Youri Tielemans, Mason Mount, Leny Yoro, Noussair Mazraoui and Diogo Dalot.

The identical twins Jack and Tyler Fletcher are split between the two groups, with Pochettino's assistant Jesus Perez across both.

Not all the players were identifiable and United confirmed defender Patrick Dorgu was involved.

title: Anthropic keeps the AI party swinging, but the atmosphere is bubbly | Nils Pratley
author: Nils Pratley
text:
Can the newly listed AI company really be worth $2tn? Anyone who remembers the late 1990s has good reason to ask

R oll up, roll up, who wants to buy shares in a company whose technology “could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”, as the prospectus had it? Virtually everybody, as it turned out. Anthropic flew out of the blocks on its first day as a listed company .

From the point of view of the promoters, the result was as good as it gets. The final pricing for the shares at $83 apiece was meaningfully higher than the indicated range of $70 to $78, but still left room for a big initial “pop”. There were positive vibes all round – especially for the battalion of investment banks collecting $550m of underwriting fees .

And, to be fair, it wasn’t nailed-on that the show would go so swimmingly. There was a late risk that investor sentiment towards the AI universe could be jinxed – or Jensened – by the soap opera at Nvidia . More generally, there was a worry that the AI bubble, if that’s what it is, could burst when somebody tried to unload too much stock on the stock market in one go.

Anthropic, though, has set records by raising $107bn. It is an extraordinary sum, especially for a business founded five years ago. At the listing price, Anthropic was valued at $1.5tn. When shares began trading at £111.50, its market capitalisation was up to $2tn. Only 14 months ago, it raised money at a valuation of a “mere” $183bn .

The feat, though, is not wholly inexplicable. Some $26bn of the listing proceeds were virtually in the bag, thanks to the cornerstone placement to AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC. That assembly of AI and AI-adjacent names fed worries about the industry’s circular financing.

But, on the other hand, every fund manager knew he or she would be betting against the crowd by saying no. Momentum can carry a stock a long way, even before the index funds and index-hugging funds are obliged to buy (Nasdaq entry will be quick; the S&P 500 will take at least a year).

Take a step back, though, and ask whether Anthropic – loss-making and with projected revenues in 2026 of $50bn-ish – can possibly be worth $1.5tn-plus.

The short, and unhelpful, answer is that virtually any valuation could be made to sound plausible if you believe, first, that AI is a generational technology that will be adopted at never-seen-before speed and, second, that “frontier” pioneering firms, of which Anthropic is the leader, will capture an outsized slice of the commercial value for years and years.

Consider the assumptions behind that thesis, however. Can Anthropic really improve from $50bn-ish of revenue this year to $600bn in 2030, which is roughly what tech analysts have pencilled in? Given the current rate of growth, perhaps it can. But sustaining the pace, or something like it, for another 16 quarters simply won’t be straightforward or mechanical.

What is the real level of demand from corporate users for frontier models? Nobody doubts that AI adoption is still in the early stage, but does everybody need the finest product from Anthropic’s Claude suite? Already executives grumble that their IT budgets are finite and that nine-month-old versions, or cheaper “open weight” models from rivals, do the job for basic work. Lasting pricing power in AI is simply unclear. “Commoditisation risk”, in the jargon, could be the next year’s valuation debate.

Then there is the investment bill to make it all happen – $900bn of spending commitments were detailed in the prospectus for computing power and infrastructure. The listing proceeds help, as does the visibility and credibility that comes with being on a public market. But debt, not just equity, will be a crucial part of this story.

“Obviously, at some point in the future we’re hoping to be investment grade,” said co-founder Dario Amodei as trading in the shares started. You bet: the price at which Anthropic borrows matters fundamentally.

Away from the party atmosphere, the European Central Bank has its eye on financial stability in the eurozone. This week, it issued one of those fuddy-duddy reminders about how much capital is being bet on the AI revolution , and how little transparency there is around the funding of hyperscalers and other suppliers to the boom.

“Big tech firms are estimated to have total off-balance-sheet commitments of more than $4tn as of the second quarter of 2026,” its report said, warning of “historical parallels with the dotcom and sub-prime bubbles”.

It is not the only one to see warning signs. Anthropic is an astonishingly successful company already and is plainly at the forefront of a significant technological shift. But it has been listed in an environment that looks – to most of us who remember the late 1990s and the subsequent bust – to have bubbly characteristics. AI technology, like the internet, is gamechanging. But it doesn’t mean today’s share prices are right.

title: Myanmar ruling gives new relevance to genocide convention and is ‘full of messages’ for Israel
author: Julian Borger
text:
Hailed as ‘a rare moment of justice’, judges’ decision sets out a roadmap for assessing the question of intent

The international court of justice (ICJ) verdict making Myanmar the first country in history to be found guilty of committing genocide does not just deliver justice for Rohingya victims. It also gives the 1948 genocide convention new relevance in governing the actions of nation states.

In their nine votes to six majority ruling, the panel of judges in The Hague set out a detailed roadmap for how the convention should be applied to real-world situations in which a government is accused of committing genocide against a whole population group, especially when it comes to assessing the question of intent.

The lengthy judgment will have been read particularly carefully by Israel, the only other country currently before the ICJ accused of genocide.

It is also relevant to Germany, which has been brought before the court by Nicaragua on the accusation it has facilitated and failed to prevent genocide in Gaza.

“I think it’s a judgment that brings the genocide convention alive,” said Philippe Sands, a leading human rights lawyer who was part of the Gambian legal team. “It gives the convention practical, real meaning. And if the alternative view had been taken, the convention would essentially become a dead letter.”

Amnesty International’s secretary general, Agnès Callamard, called the ruling “a rare moment of justice for survivors, victims and their families”. But it was also an assertion of humanitarian law in an increasingly lawless world.

“This is a good day for international law. We needed it,” said Dr Iva Vukušić, an assistant professor in international History at Utrecht University and a war crimes expert. “It is really important, clarifying a lot of law, and that’s going to be very helpful going forward.”

There will be a spillover from this ruling to its sister tribunal in The Hague, the international criminal court (ICC), providing a benchmark for when genocide charges could be made against individual perpetrators.

The Trump administration, instinctively hostile to international legal institutions, is also watching critically. The US ambassador to the UN told the ICJ before this judgment not to “lower the legal threshold for proving genocide” lest it be “weaponised” against US and allied soldiers.

The court did not directly lower the standard for demonstrating genocide, and the Gambia – which brought the case to The Hague – did not ask it to.

The judges kept the existing benchmark for judging genocide intent as the “only reasonable inference” of Myanmar’s actions and referred extensively to prior case law. But it went a long way towards clarifying how that standard should be applied in assessing atrocity crimes committed by states.

Before this case, only Serbia had faced the charge of genocide at the ICJ, in cases brought by Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the Bosnian ruling in 2007 , Belgrade was found to have failed to prevent the 1995 genocide in Srebrenica, but in both cases it was cleared of committing the genocide directly.

The new ICJ judgment finds the Myanmar military directly responsible for genocide against the Rohingya , a Muslim minority targeted in a ferocious counterinsurgency campaign that reached its peak in 2017.

In assessing the Myanmar campaign, the ICJ looked not just at the death toll of about 10,000 in assessing the scale of the atrocities, but at the total Rohingya population targeted in northern Rakhine state, 815,000 people. Significantly, it cast its net wider than just the death toll, considering mental damage done to the survivors, particularly victims of sexual violence, and the impact on reproduction in the Rohingya community.

Most importantly, the ICJ judgment provided a guide to interpreting the standard set by Serbian cases, in which a finding of genocide could be made only if there were not other plausible motives for mass killing.

In this judgment, the court ruled that Myanmar could have had other motives, such as the desire to displace or punish the Rohingya population, but that those motives could exist alongside genocidal intent. The judges said genocidal intent was the “only reasonable inference” from the “totality” of evidence.

In justifying that conclusion the judges pointed to several factors that international law experts say are relevant to the Gaza case, which is now hearing written pleadings and is expected to take at least another three years.

The common factors include the targeting of children, which the court described as striking at the “foundation” of the Rohingya as a group – the ICJ said up to 2,109 Rohingya children under the age of five had been killed, while more than 5,000 Palestinian children under five years old have been killed in the Gaza war.

Another incriminating factor cited by the court was the “bulldozing and large-scale terrain clearance” after the destruction of villages, followed by “rapid construction” including security installations, which has been the hallmark of Israeli army occupation of over 60% of the Gaza Strip.

“It’s full of messages for Israel,” said William Schabas, an international law professor and expert on genocide at Middlesex University. “There are obvious differences, of course, the evidence will be different, but if you exchanged the word Myanmar with Israel, you wouldn’t have to change much in the judgment.”

The fact that there were six dissenting voices on the bench suggested that substantial parts of the majority’s reasoning were not beyond dispute, and lawyers involved in the case cautioned that it did not necessarily mean that the same bench would find Israel guilty of genocide in Gaza. But the same lawyers added that the opposite was almost certainly true. If this case had failed, the case brought by South Africa against Israel would have been all but over.

title: China, Russia and US agree peace declaration with no mention of Ukraine and Iran wars
author: Rebecca Bailey in Shenzhen
text:
Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’

China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.

The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.

The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.

The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.

“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”

Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and now had a “mutual understanding”.

Some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed Trump’s advances to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.

The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK.

“The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” said Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.

Analysts had said that the meeting’s primary significance was in its optics. “Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,” said Prof William Hurst, from the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back at the suggestion the summit had just been a photo-op. “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said.

In the declaration, the men “committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security”.

First among their concerns was “promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”. Sun said this was a favourite topic of China’s and showed that Beijing was “flexing its diplomatic muscles”. She said: “It is able to set the agenda and the deliverables according to its priorities … and make other great powers accept them.”

The declaration also agreed that “the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant and so the clause added to the perception that he has done well from the summit. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian president has been treated as an international pariah by Kyiv’s allies and he has not been to an Apec summit in years.

Hurst said: “This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power. It’s yet another example of Putin playing a poor hand to maximum effect.”

Xi, his status as a global power broker now assured, began the morning by addressing Apec leaders, reiterating the themes of trade openness and innovation he has emphasised throughout the summit. However, Apec affairs appeared to take a back seat for most of the day, with business dominating the discussions. For all the camaraderie on display, relations are complex. Russia is under US sanctions over the Ukraine war, while China and the US spent much of the last year engaged in an escalating tit-for-tat trade war before Trump and Xi called a truce .

Trump and Putin earlier held a separate meeting – their first since August 2025 – where the US president called his Russian counterpart his “friend”.

European allies meeting in Berlin to show their support for Ukraine expressed indignation at the cosy optics. “Mr Putin is not our friend and ⁠will never be,” the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said in a rejoinder to Trump. The Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, said she found it “very incomprehensible” that a US ​president would want to sit down with Putin.

The peace declaration in Shenzhen said the three countries planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. That was important, said Shan Guo from Hutong Research, a Shanghai-based advisory firm, but “now let’s see if the US will lift sanctions”.

Trump and Xi then held their third bilateral of this year. Xi said the US-China relationship was “generally stable and positive”, according to state media. But he cautioned Washington over Taiwan, saying the US “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in US-China relations”.

Another watched-for topic lacking detailed findings was that of AI. Xi said the two countries should “enhance communication and coordination to guard against security risks … and ensure that AI remains under human control at all times”.

Ultimately, the lack of breakthroughs might suit China, which has no appetite to move beyond the role of convener, said Kim. “Beijing has little interest in taking on the diplomatic risks of brokering an actual peace agreement in Ukraine or resolving the conflict with Iran. That would entangle China in conflicts it would rather avoid,” she said.

title: Trump accused of falling asleep during Xi Jinping speech at Apec summit in China
author: Ariana Baio
text:
US president appeared to doze off while Chinese leader made speech, but White House insisted he was awake

Donald Trump was, again, accused of falling asleep during a televised event, this time during the speech of the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in China.

The US president appeared to close his eyes for roughly 10 seconds on Thursday. As his eyes closed, Trump’s head tilted downward, and his hands remained clasped in front of him.

Several prominent Trump critics on social media alleged that the US president was asleep, including Republicans Against Trump , California governor Gavin Newsom’s press office and conservative lawyer George Conway .

White House officials denied the allegations, claiming the 80-year-old US president was looking down at papers in front of him.

“Fake News! President Trump was looking at papers in front of him while the speaker made remarks. You can clearly see his eyes move back and forth,” Steven Cheung, the White House director of communications, wrote on X in response to a Newsweek article.

“This is why the people despise media so much. They constantly lie,” Cheung added.

Trump often faces accusations of falling asleep during televised events such as Oval Office press conferences, cabinet meetings and sporting events.

Occasionally, while listening to other people speak, the US president will close his eyes for several seconds, appearing as though he is falling asleep . Despite footage of the instances going viral, the White House and Trump allies have insisted the US president does not fall asleep during meetings.

Administration officials have excused Trump’s apparent drowsiness as blinking or an example of the president listening intently. They consistently claim Trump “doesn’t sleep”.

Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, testified to lawmakers earlier this year that he had “never seen” Trump fall asleep.

“On the contrary, the guy doesn’t sleep, which is a big problem because he calls me at two in the morning,” Rubio said in June.

Last year, JD Vance said that Trump hardly ever sleeps, even while traveling overnight.

“If we go on a 20-hour trip somewhere, he doesn’t sleep the entire time. And of course, if he’s not sleeping, if he’s working, he expects everybody else to be working too,” Vance told Fox News .

Trump became the oldest US president ever inaugurated when he was sworn in nearly two years ago. Despite his age, Trump often claims he is in near-perfect health , often bragging about his “perfect” cognitive test results and insisting he has a lot of energy.

title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘It’s going to be bittersweet’
author: Antonio Losada
text:
Revenge game for KAT today?

I don’t think so, but who knows.

Here’s the latest before visiting the Wolves in still-not-overly-cold Minnesota.

On Rick Brunson’s decision to bring Jose Alvarado into the game against Toronto:

“Just a great call. Rick Brunson made the call of throwing Jose in to see if he can give us a spark. So, just a heckuva call by Rick Brunson and just a fantastic job by Jose producing on both sides of the ball when his name was called.”

On Karl-Anthony Towns improving his passing decisions and avoiding risks:

“It’s a fine balance because he’s capable of making some beautiful passes in tight windows so you want to let him be him. But I thought earlier in the year — and we talked to him about it, and said it a couple times — he was trying to make the home-run pass a little too much.

“And he’s gotten to a point where he’s mixing it up now. We’re going to trust him because he’s obviously done it for many years now with good results. We’ll lean on him quite a bit in that regard but if we turn the ball over too much, we’ll let him know.”

On Towns’ basketball intelligence and ability to read the game:

“KAT’s got tremendous feel. He’s a smart, smart dude when it comes to a lot of things, but especially when it comes to the game of basketball.”

On Towns’ coachability and the impact of assistant coaches Brendan O’Connor and Darren Erman:

“It’s easy to see where he is, because everything we’ve asked him to do, he’s tried to do. So, you’re extremely coachable. You got a great feel. And you got two guys in (assistant coaches) Brendan O’Connor and Darren Erman that are teaching you the game defensively at a really high level, and you’re starting to see the results of it.”

On the Knicks’ execution and contributions throughout the roster against Toronto:

“Our execution was at an extremely high level. We had a lot of guys contribute in a lot of ways tonight.”

On the Knicks early-season woes:

“It’s still a work in progress.”

On why the NBA must continue penalizing dangerous closeouts and landing-space violations after Brunson’s injury scare:

“They got to keep track of it because it’s going to happen. Everybody wants to try to block [Brunson’s] shot and every other guy’s shot. Some guys go forward too much and, if they do, there’s got to be a heavy penalty. Because if there’s no heavy penalty, then guys won’t be conscious of it. They’ll just keep sliding underneath guys.”

On why his shooting technique sometimes exposes him to dangerous situations:

“I fade a little bit. Taller guys are usually guarding me, so I got to be able to fade a little bit. Sometimes they’re not jumping straight up. They’re jumping towards me. It happens.”

On prioritizing getting buckets over worrying about landing on a defender’s foot:

“I’m not worried about falling on his foot. I’m more worried about if he’s close enough to block it. If he is too close, I probably won’t shoot it. If he’s not, ball is going up.”

On the Knicks rediscovering their preferred style of play against Toronto:

“We just played to the best of our abilities. I know the early season hasn’t looked like it, but that’s how we’re most comfortable.”

On the disappointment of not winning a championship during his nine seasons in Minnesota:

“I wanted to win one there. I didn’t accomplish that. But it was great to have those moments, to bring Minnesota back to the playoffs and be able to do a lot of things.”

On returning to Minnesota as an NBA champion with the Knicks:

“It’s going to be bittersweet. I’m just happy that I have such amazing fans and had such an amazing time in Minnesota. I love it to death. I love that place so it’s going to be cool to go back.”

On becoming a minority owner of Napoli’s basketball team:

“Napoli is a great underdog story and reminds me of what we have built with the Knicks in many ways. It is a project built around hard work, big dreams and the incredible passion Napoli fans have for their team. I’ve been coming to Naples and the Amalfi Coast for years, and I know what a fan base like this can mean to a team. Seeing this club already making noise in the EuroCup tells you where it’s headed.

“Matt Rizzetta and the team at Underdog Global Partners have high ambitions with a real plan for where this club is going. The Napoli journey is still very much in the first quarter, so I am excited to be a part of building this into something truly special in the years ahead.”

On Instagram after being demoted from starting center to the second unit:

“Nobody gone save me, gotta save my damn self.”

title: Demi Vollering, Eddy Merckx, Paul Seixas among cycling stars set for audience with Pope Leo XIV
author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
text:
A host of representatives from the cycling world, including Demi Vollering , Eddy Merckx, and Paul Seixas , will attend an audience with Pope Leo XIV at the Vatican next week.

UCI President David Lappartient described the November 23 event as "an opportunity to strengthen cycling's commitment, as a sport, to promoting peace and intercultural dialogue among peoples."

Past and present Grand Tour champions are among a group of over 100 "distinguished guests" attending, in addition to organisers of all men's and women's Grand Tours and other races, and representatives from various cycling federations.

Vollering, Merckx, and Seixas will be joined by a host of current and former road riders, including Bernard Hinault, Annemiek van Vleuten, Greg LeMond, Elisa Longo Borghini, Francesco Moser, Miguel Indurain, Jeannie Longo, Vincenzo Nibali, Chris Froome , and Mark Cavendish.

Multiple para-cycling world champion Ricardo Ten Argilés, multiple BMX world champion Mariana Pajón, and Ukrainian cyclist Anna Kolyzhuk, who suffered a serious spinal injury in a crash during a race this year, will also attend.

Ahead of the event, Lappartient "highlighted the longstanding historical roots between cycling and the Catholic Church, from races organised by parish communities and cycling teams inspired by Gospel values, to the various meetings with Popes throughout the 20th century and the recent passage of the Giro d’Italia through the Vatican during the 2025 Jubilee."

The event will see Pope Leo XIV take an audience with the riders before the UCI symbolically donates several bicycles to Caritas Rome, a charitable organisation founded by the Episcopal Conference of Italy.

The audience isn't the first time the Pope and the cycling world have come together. In 2025, the Pope blessed the peloton ahead of the final stage of the Giro d'Italia, which started in the Vatican. The stage was dedicated to Pope Francis, who died in April.

Several other Popes have addressed the Giro in the past, including Pope Paul VI in 1964 and Pope John Paul II in 2000. Pope John Paul II also offered his support to the Amore e Vita cycling team in the 1990s and 2000s.

title: ‘Everyone struggled for this justice’: tears in court as Rohingya vindicated in Myanmar genocide ruling
author: Kaamil Ahmed in The Hague and Yassin Abdumonab in Cox's Bazar
text:
Relief in the immediate aftermath of a landmark ruling, but what happens next is in the hands of governments around the world

There were tears in the halls of The Hague in the Netherlands and an eruption of applause in the refugee camps of Bangladesh as the scattered communities of Rohingya watched the UN’s top court rule the Myanmar military had committed genocide against them.

For almost a decade, the Rohingya have awaited this moment; recognition from the international court of justice (ICJ) that Myanmar in 2017 intentionally tried to destroy the mostly Muslim minority group through a campaign of mass killings and rape. More than 10,000 Rohingya were killed and 700,000 fled to neighbouring Bangladesh .

By the time they spilled into the court’s halls, the relief was evident. A Rohingya community leader threw a big thumbs up as he left the courtroom and others immediately took out their phones to call family in the refugee camps.

Salma, 30, a Rohingya survivor who lost family members in the 2017 genocide, said: “Everyone worked hard and struggled for this justice, for this cause. When they hear it today, everyone will be happy, thank God. I don’t know how to express it or even what to do with myself.”

Another Rohingya present, who cannot be named because of safety concerns, said they cried as the judge went through each of the rulings.

“During the last few minutes I couldn’t even sit down any more, I had to move to the back because I didn’t know how I’d react,” they said. “I saw some of the other Rohingya around me crying. They were so emotional.

“Now the responsibility is with the international governments. It has been declared genocide now and they have to act.”

In Bangladesh, where most of the Rohingya population have lived – in the world’s largest refugee camp – since being forced to flee in 2017, the verdict was translated into the Rohingya language for the crowds who had gathered to watch on screens specially set up for the purpose.

They immediately leapt up, cheering, applauding and shouting gratitude for the Gambia – the faraway African nation that brought the case to the ICJ on behalf of the stateless minority. Many held posters that read “Thank You Gambia” and “Justice = Safe Return”.

“Since we arrived here, we have been waiting and looking forward to this justice,” said Farida Khatun, 50, who has been a refugee in Bangladesh since 2017, when her village, Tula Toli, was targeted by soldiers. The village in north-western Myanmar, near the Bangladesh border, was the scene of a massacre in August of that year, with reports of mass killings and gang rapes .

She said, however, that she does not expect to be able to return home. Tula Toli was completely destroyed by Myanmar’s forces and no longer exists. “Even though today’s verdict makes us happy, my heart still cannot believe that they will take us back in true peace.”

The case has taken seven years to reach this point, with Rohingya researchers working to collect testimony from survivors. The initial hope for justice had faded during the long wait for a ruling. Many were also left deflated during early hearings when the one-time pro-democracy hero Aung San Suu Kyi defended the Myanmar military at The Hague.

Before today’s ruling, some were optimistic, others were prepared to be disappointed, but all said they knew themselves that they were victims of genocide.

The tension was finally released when the court declared Myanmar was responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, highlighting the use of sexual violence and attacks on children alongside the killing of Rohingya who tried to flee violence, which it said meant the violence amounted to more than ethnic cleansing.

The court ordered Myanmar to provide reparations for the Rohingya and end continuing breaches of the genocide convention.

There is now also an international criminal court investigation into the violence of 2017, looking specifically at the crime of mass deportation, and for which prosecutors in 2024 sought an arrest warrant for Myanmar’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing.

With continuing violence against the Rohingya , the possibility of a return to Myanmar, as happened after previous exoduses to Bangladesh in 1978 and the early 1990s, remains unlikely.

But many hope the ICJ ruling will be the start of a process of ensuring justice and lead to real international pressure to ensure their safety in Myanmar.

“We will be able to return to our homeland – with our rights, with our citizenship, and having received our full security. We will be able to return,” says Salma.

title: Anthropic raises $81bn in record-breaking stock market debut
text:
Anthropic is poised to hit a value of more than $1.4 trillion (£1.1 trillion) when it debuts on the public stock market.

The artificial intelligence (AI) company behind the popular chatbot Claude said it will price shares at $83 each when it lists on Thursday on the Nasdaq, a tech-focused stock exchange based in New York.

That price will make it one of the most highly valued companies in the world.

It will be the first US firm focused exclusively on AI to go public, marking a crucial test for the fast-growing industry, which faces questions over whether the huge investment poured into the technology will be profitable.

The AI firm said earlier this month it would likely offer its shares for between $70 and $78 each, which valued the company at up to $1.3tn.

But demand for Anthropic's stock debut - commonly referred to as its initial public offering, or IPO - is very high, according to one early investor in the company who spoke with the BBC on condition of anonymity.

The person said shares were more than 10 times oversubscribed ahead of the public listing, meaning demand for Anthropic shares exceeded the number of shares available.

If that turns out to be the case, Anthropic's valuation could quickly blow past its target on Thursday when trading begins.

Depending on how strong that demand is, Anthropic could even exceed the early market valuation of Elon Musk's SpaceX, which was the world's most highly valued stock debut when it went public with a value of $2.2tn in June.

However, in the weeks that followed, SpaceX shares fell significantly in price .

As it stands, Anthropic's listing will see the firm raise more than $68bn from its initial investors. It is also expecting another $26bn from private placements. So the total amount the company will raise is expected to be $94bn.

The amount of cash Anthropic has raised from its listing is already more than SpaceX raised in June .

OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT and Anthropic's biggest AI rival, is expected to go public next year.

Until then, Anthropic will be the only public company in the US that is entirely focused on the technology, or one that was founded and built around AI tools and products. Its scope is different from tech giants like Google and Microsoft that also develop AI but are involved in other tech services.

The seven Anthropic founders who are about to become multi-billionaires

There is excitement around Anthropic's listing, but also some concern from investors around its ability to generate revenue and profits going forward.

Yang Wang, a principle financial analyst with Counterpoint Research, said the central issue for Anthropic is whether its business "can keep pace" as hundreds of billions of dollars in financial obligations come due in the next couple of years.

"Nevertheless, it is not an everyday occurrence for public investors to gain direct exposure to a frontier-model developer with the potential to shape the next stage of productivity," Wang said.

While nearly every other major tech company is pouring huge amounts of money into the technology and infrastructure required for their own AI tools, they are built around social media or online retail or online search. AI tools and applications are secondary.

"Anthropic going public gives us a whole new window into what AI demand looks like," Marta Norton, who heads investment strategy at investment firm Empower, told the BBC.

Anthropic was started by a group of co-founders , led by siblings Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei, all of whom left their work at OpenAI to start a new AI firm.

The company has carved itself out in the ongoing AI race as more focused on building the technology with safety top of mind.

It refused to comply with a demand by the US Department of Defense that Anthropic's tools be used in an essentially unrestricted way. And Dario Amodei has been outspoken in his belief that AI tools may soon be so powerful that they present a threat to human existence.

Nonetheless, the company is looking to grow quickly and gain more access to financing through the public markets in order to do so.

Norton said Anthropic going public now, in a time of market volatility comes down to the simple fact that the company needs access to more money.

"AI is financially demanding," Norton said. "The public markets open up the financial spigot a little bit more, and so the time has come."

But broader anxieties have started to grow about the AI industry's business model, which is reliant on expensive computer chips that are in short supply. The technology is also dependent on controversial data centres and funding such operations require deals with other tech companies.

The Federal Reserve Bank has expressed concern about the rapid growth of AI-related debt being financed through "complex and opaque" structures, according to minutes from its October meeting to discuss a potential rate rise.

A few of the meeting's participants also noted that "AI-related exposures were becoming increasingly concentrated among a small number of firms".

title: Polygon’s Fastest Gravel Bike To Date
author: Alison Jaksen
text:
Polygon's new Tambora gravel bike. (Photo: Polygon Bikes)

Since 1989, manufacturing and development has been in Polygon Bikes’ DNA. The Indonesia-based factory brand is in a country shaped by tremendous geological forces. The island nation’s massive volcanoes have reformed the landscape countless times and created awe-inspiring topography.

The lesson: Change is good. Polygon focused on a clear priority with the evolution of the all-new Tambora: speed. This is the fastest gravel bike the company has produced, with design elements that let riders push their routes faster and further than ever. Compared to the previous version of the Tambora, the front end is 32mm lower, while the head angle slackens by 0.8 degrees. Those tweaks improve aerodynamics for both bike and rider, while the longer wheelbase and chainstays create more stability when you’re charging down the trail.

​Adding to the Tambora’s race-ready performance: its frame. The frame’s ACX carbon-fiber construction takes inspiration from its Helios road bike sibling—designed to excel at power transfer while reducing ride fatigue. The bike also boasts 55c tire clearance and is compatible with 1x and 2x drivetrains. If more rugged terrain calls to you, the Tambora is also compatible with aftermarket suspension forks up to 40mm of travel, without changing the current geometry.

​While speed is this bike’s specialty, it also features the thoughtful, rider-friendly design elements Polygon is known for. The new Tambora takes full advantage of the brand’s PolyPocket internal frame storage, which offers a full downtube width opening for easy access. This soft-sided, zippered pouch holds tools, snacks, and other essentials in a convenient, low-profile package. Up in the cockpit, a Fidlock mount recessed into the top tube makes it quick and easy to connect your preferred accessories, while keeping everything tight when you ratchet up the RPMs.

Also great: The value proposition for Polygon Bikes is as good as the performance. The Tambora series starts at $1,799, with a wide range of competitively priced options. The Tambora 7 Di2 ($2,999) and Tambora 9 AXS with SRAM Force ($4,499) are particularly good deals considering the specs.

Put it all together and you have a bike that’s both fast and capable of serious saddle time—and comes at sweet price. With four models across six frame sizes, there’s a redesigned Tambora for every gravel rider who wants to experience the wonders of evolution for themselves.

Founded in 1989, Polygon began with a simple belief: Great bikes shouldn’t be out of reach. What started as a small OEM operation has grown through decades of building, experimenting, and refining bikes for real riders—experiences that still define the global brand today.

title: ‘Pot luck service’: Royal Mail on course to miss delivery targets for fourth year in a row
author: Lauren Almeida
text:
Citizens Advice criticises company for failing to meet Ofcom requirements while reporting increased revenue

Royal Mail has been accused of offering a “pot luck service” to consumers as it looks likely to miss first-class delivery targets for the fourth consecutive year.

The postal service, whose parent company was bought for £3.6bn by the Czech billionaire Daniel Křetínský last year, is meant to deliver 90% of its first-class post by the next working day and 95% of second-class post within three working days according to targets set by the regulator, Ofcom.

But it delivered only 82.5% of first-class mail within target in the second quarter of this year, down from 85% in the first quarter. Second-class deliveries slipped to 87.2% arriving within three working days, compared with 91.4% in the previous quarter.

On Thursday, Royal Mail said it did not expect to meet its targets until next April. It last met its first-class delivery target in 2017, before they were temporarily suspended during the pandemic.

Tom MacInnes, the director of policy at the charity Citizens Advice, said: “Putting a letter in a postbox shouldn’t be like rolling a dice to see if it arrives on time.

“But that’s the pot luck service consumers get with Royal Mail.”

Royal Mail has been fined a total of £37m since 2023 for missing delivery targets set by Ofcom. In June, the regulator launched an investigation into the company for the missed targets, saying it would investigate whether the company was prioritising parcel delivery over letters, a practice alleged by whistleblowers and unions but denied by the company.

The postal service is preparing for its busiest period of the year, beginning with the Black Friday shopping event in the run-up to Christmas.

“It is not really Black Friday any more, it’s like a Black Friday month,” said Martin Seidenberg, the chief executive of Royal Mail’s parent company International Distribution Services (IDS). He added that it was “already quite busy in the network”, but said “we are ready”.

Royal Mail said on Thursday it had hired an additional 22,000 seasonal workers and was ready for “a very busy Christmas”.

On the same day, IDS reported a 6.3% rise in revenue to £6.85bn in the six months to 27 September. Royal Mail’s revenue rose 3.9% to £4.13bn.

The number of letters being sent through Royal Mail has more than halved in the past decade, falling from about 20bn to 6.7bn. The number of addresses it serves has gone up by 4m in the same period.

The company has continued to miss performance targets despite Ofcom giving it permission last year to downgrade its universal service obligation . This has meant a reduction in second-class deliveries to alternate weekdays, with no second-class deliveries on Saturdays.

In April, Royal Mail faced criticism for raising the price of a first-class stamp by 10p , or 6%, to £1.80, and a second-class stamp by 4p, or 5%, to 91p. It blamed the increases on the “continued rise in the cost of delivery for every letter”.

The business has announced plans to cut up to 2,500 jobs as part of an effort to restructure, with a focus on head office and “support function roles”. It last made a big round of cuts in 2022 , when it said it was looking to eliminate up to 10,000 roles, including 6,000 full-time frontline jobs.

A spokesperson said: “Royal Mail is broadly on track to deliver against its quality of service improvement plan with first-class next-working-day performance up 9.1 percentage points on last year and ahead of the trajectory set out in the plan.

“Taking into account the emergency exemption to regulatory quality of service targets during the pandemic, Royal Mail has missed its regulatory targets for the last four years.”

title: ‘Should Manchester United fans be hoping for relegation?’ Will Unwin answered your questions
author: Will Unwin and Guardian moderators
text:
Manchester United have a new head coach. Mauricio Pochettino has signed a two-and-a-half-year deal to replace Michael Carrick, who was sacked after leading the club to their worst start to a season in four decades.

In a tearful farewell to the US men’s national team, Pochettino called the move “one of the most difficult decisions” of his career. But the job he inherits may be harder still. No team in Europe’s top five leagues has conceded more goals in all competitions this season. Bruno Fernandes has rejected a second offer of a new contract. And fans have turned their anger on the hierarchy above the dugout.

In his analysis of what the new head coach must do, Will Unwin wrote that whoever took over would have to find solutions on the pitch while putting pressure on those above him: “United fans know the person in the dugout cannot take all the blame and someone else has to be publicly accountable.”

Pochettino’s first game is at Liverpool on Sunday, then Sporting away in the Champions League. So is he the right man for the job? Can he get a tune out of this squad, and who will thrive under his high-intensity style? And will the club’s owners give him the time and the tools he needs?

Will, who covers Manchester United for the Guardian, will be live here at 2pm GMT on Thursday 19 November to answer your questions.
